direct_answer: Losing a partner or close person can bring grief alongside practical changes, such as living alone for the first time. With arthritis and frailty, everyday tasks and safety may need planning. Support is available from your GP, bereavement services and local groups.

content:
Grief affects body and mind. Pain, sleep and energy can all be harder after a loss.

This guide covers grief and practical steps. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Grief and your health

Grief can affect sleep, appetite and pain. It is normal. Tell your GP if you are struggling.

Practical safety when living alone

  • Consider a personal alarm.
  • Keep a phone within reach.
  • Arrange regular contact with someone.
  • Plan what to do if you fall.

Tasks the other person did

Ask family, friends or the council for help with tasks you now do alone.

Staying connected

  • Bereavement groups.
  • Lunch clubs.
  • Social prescribing.

Getting support

Your GP can refer you for talking therapies or bereavement support.

When to get help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you or someone else is in danger. You can also call Samaritans on 116 123.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it normal to feel more pain?

Grief can make pain feel worse.

When should I seek help?

If you feel unable to cope or have thoughts of harming yourself, get help.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Grief after bereavement or loss
  • NHS: NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression

Living With Arthritis is an independent charity and is not part of Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). Everyone's situation is different, so follow the advice of your own GP and care team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
